titre: Where the Eel Is Born: A Century-Old Deduction, With No Egg to Back It Up
accroche: Since the 1920s, its birth has been placed in the Sargasso Sea. As of 2022, no egg or breeding adult had yet been collected there.
contenu_vulgarise:
Adult eels are caught in the rivers of Europe, but where they reproduce has remained a mystery. According to the researchers who are taking up the question today, it has intrigued generations, from Aristotle to Freud.

## An Answer Deduced from the Size of Larvae

In the early 20th century, the Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt attacks the problem from the other end. The eel goes through a larval stage, the leptocephalus. Schmidt and his teams catch them across the Atlantic, notably, from 1920 to 1922, in three cruises of the ship Dana funded by the Carlsberg Foundation. They note one decisive point: the smallest larvae, and so the youngest, are concentrated in the Sargasso Sea, in the middle of the North Atlantic, very far from the rivers of Europe and North Africa. He concludes that the spawning area is a restricted region of the western Atlantic, northeast and north of the West Indies, because that is where, he writes, the youngest larvae are found.

It is detective reasoning: you follow the trail of the smallest individuals back to the place where they were born. More recent surveys have found larvae under 12 millimeters, less than twenty days old, over a band about 2,000 kilometers wide, and even younger ones, under 7 millimeters, mostly between 24° and 31° north latitude, from 70° to 50° west longitude.

## What No One Has Seen

Here is the point that remains open. Nearly a hundred years after Schmidt, researchers were still writing, in 2022, that no egg and no breeding adult has ever been collected in the Sargasso Sea. The adult, however, does make the journey: 5,000 to 10,000 kilometers across the Atlantic, the longest breeding migration of any eel.

In 2018 and 2019, a team fitted satellite tags to 26 silver eels, caught in the Azores and presumed to be females based on their size, about 2,500 kilometers from the eastern edge of the presumed area. Twenty-three tags transmitted, twenty-one delivered substantial data, for 40 to 366 days, at an average speed of 6.5 to 6.8 kilometers per day (the article gives both values). Five of the tags' pop-up positions were within the limits of the Sargasso Sea, and one eel was in the presumed spawning area. The authors see in this the first direct evidence that an adult eel reaches this place.

## What This Changes

Here is the shift: what is taken for granted in a textbook can rest, for a century, on an inference, solid but indirect. Schmidt deduced where the spawning area is; he did not see the birth. The tags filled part of the gap: adults do reach the region, and a single eel ended up in the presumed spawning area. What remains is the spawning itself, which no one has observed. The recruitment of the European eel has fallen by 95% since the 1980s, attributed in part to factors in its life at sea: what is a protection worth that still ignores where, and how, the species reproduces?

repere.texte: Of 26 silver eels tagged from the Azores in 2018 and 2019, 21 tags delivered data (40 to 366 days): five pop-up positions were within the limits of the Sargasso Sea, one in the presumed spawning area. As of 2022, no egg or breeding adult had been collected there.
repere.source: Wright et al., “First direct evidence of adult European eels migrating to their breeding place in the Sargasso Sea,” Scientific Reports 12, 2022

carte.punch: Schmidt placed the eel's birth in the Sargasso Sea. No egg has been seen there.
carte.idee: The Sargasso Sea has been named since the 1920s as the birthplace of the European eel, based on the size of the larvae. As of 2022, no egg or breeding adult had been collected there; satellite tags have shown that adults reach the region.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Schmidt, “The breeding places of the eel,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, vol. 211, pp. 179-208
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The original paper, the reference for the spawning area deduced from the larvae.

quiz.question: What is the designation of the Sargasso Sea as the birthplace of the European eel based on?
choix: On eggs and breeding adults collected on site
On satellite tags tracking adults from the coasts of Europe
On the size of the larvae, the smallest being found in that area
On fishermen who saw the eels spawning off the West Indies
quiz.explication: Schmidt followed the trail of the smallest larvae back to the Sargasso Sea; it is an inference. Eggs and breeding adults have never been collected there, and the 2018-2019 tags show only that adults arrive there.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which ship conducted the larva-fishing cruises led by Johannes Schmidt between 1920 and 1922?
choix: The Dana, funded by the Carlsberg Foundation
The Beagle, chartered by the Royal Society
The Calypso, commanded by Jacques-Yves Cousteau
The Challenger, of the British navy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Johannes Schmidt and his teams conducted three cruises of the ship Dana between 1920 and 1922, funded by the Carlsberg Foundation, to catch eel larvae across the Atlantic.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the satellite tags fitted to silver eels in 2018 and 2019 show?
choix: That no adult eel ever reaches the Sargasso Sea
That adult eels lay their eggs off the Azores
That adult eels reach the Sargasso Sea, one of them in the presumed spawning area
That the eels' migration lasts less than ten days
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Of 26 tagged eels, 21 delivered data: five pop-up positions were within the Sargasso Sea, and one in the presumed spawning area, the first direct evidence that an adult reaches this place.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By how much has the recruitment of the European eel fallen since the 1980s, according to the entry?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that the recruitment of the European eel has fallen by 95% since the 1980s, attributed in part to factors in its life at sea, still poorly understood.
